report.title: Kestrel ransomware affiliate intrusion
report.summary: An affiliate operating the Kestrel ransomware-as-a-service compromised a logistics company through RDP password spraying on RDS-01, established silent AnyDesk remote access, disabled Microsoft Defender exclusions and real-time monitoring, dumped credentials with a renamed Mimikatz binary, exfiltrated ~310 GB of data via Rclone (disguised as svchost.exe) to Mega, and deployed the encryptor to 140 hosts using a scheduled task named 'WindowsUpdateHealth' running as SYSTEM.

behaviors.description: Threat actor performed RDP password spraying against RDS-01, generating thousands of failed logons (event 4625, LogonType 10) before a successful logon for svc_scanner from IP 185.220.101.66.
behaviors.evidence: The perimeter RDP host RDS-01 recorded over 9,000 failed logons (Windows Security event 4625, LogonType 10) from 185.220.101.0/24 across six hours, followed by a successful logon (event 4624, LogonType 10) for the account svc_scanner

behaviors.description: Operator installed AnyDesk silently via msiexec with /qn flag and configured unattended access using --set-password, creating a persistent remote-access channel not approved by the environment.
behaviors.evidence: Twenty minutes after logon the operator downloaded and installed AnyDesk silently: msiexec.exe /i C:\Users\svc_scanner\AppData\Local\Temp\AnyDesk.msi /qn

behaviors.description: Operator added Defender exclusion paths for C:\PerfLogs and C:\ProgramData\AnyDesk and disabled real-time monitoring via PowerShell, observed as Event 5007 in the Defender operational log.
Operator executed a renamed Mimikatz binary (mm.exe) from C:\PerfLogs to dump cached credentials, enabling lateral movement with domain admin adm-jpark.
behaviors.evidence: A renamed copy of Mimikatz (C:\PerfLogs\mm.exe) was executed to dump cached credentials

behaviors.description: Operator moved laterally between hosts using RDP with the domain administrator account adm-jpark, including mapping network shares (net use \\FS-02\C$ /user:CORP\adm-jpark).
behaviors.evidence: We also observed net use \\FS-02\C$ /user:CORP\adm-jpark from the RDS host

behaviors.description: Operator deleted volume shadow copies and disabled Windows recovery on each server using vssadmin, wbadmin and bcdedit commands run from cmd.exe, inhibiting system recovery before encryption.
behaviors.evidence:
vssadmin.exe delete shadows /all /quiet
wmic.exe shadowcopy delete
bcdedit.exe /set {default} bootstatuspolicy ignoreallfailures
bcdedit.exe /set {default} recoveryenabled no
wbadmin.exe delete catalog -quiet

behaviors.description: Operator exfiltrated approximately 310 GB of data using Rclone renamed to svchost.exe and placed in C:\PerfLogs, establishing TLS sessions to *.mega.co.nz on TCP/443.
behaviors.evidence: Network telemetry showed sustained TLS sessions from this process to *.mega.co.nz on TCP/443 totalling 310 GB

behaviors.description: Operator deployed the encryptor kstrl.exe to 140 hosts via SMB admin shares and executed it through a scheduled task named 'WindowsUpdateHealth' created remotely with schtasks.exe, running as SYSTEM.
Operator stopped backup and database services (MSSQLSERVER, VeeamBackupSvc, SQLWriter) using net stop commands before encryption to ensure file locks were released.
behaviors.evidence: Before encryption, the binary stopped backup and database services with net stop commands for MSSQLSERVER, VeeamBackupSvc and SQLWriter

candidates.title: Schtasks Remote Creation Of WindowsUpdateHealth Task Running Kestrel Encryptor As SYSTEM
candidates.rationale: The scheduled task 'WindowsUpdateHealth' created remotely via schtasks.exe with a masquerading name, pointing to kstrl.exe in C:\PerfLogs, running as SYSTEM on start, is highly specific to this intrusion. The combination of binary (schtasks.exe), task name, target binary path, and SYSTEM context is durable and central to the persistence stage.
candidates.false_positive_risks: Legitimate administrators might use schtasks.exe to create tasks remotely, but the task name 'WindowsUpdateHealth' masquerading as a Windows update task, the encryptor binary kstrl.exe in a non-standard path (C:\PerfLogs), and execution as SYSTEM on startup are extremely unlikely in benign activity.

candidates.title: Vssadmin Deletion Of All Shadow Copies With Quiet Flag
candidates.rationale: vssadmin.exe delete shadows /all /quiet is a precise, rarely used command that directly inhibits system recovery. The binary vssadmin.exe combined with the exact flags 'delete shadows', '/all', and '/quiet' is a strong indicator of ransomware pre-encryption preparation. This single event is sufficient for detection.
candidates.false_positive_risks: Backup software or storage admins might run vssadmin, but the '/all /quiet' combination deleting all shadows silently is atypical for legitimate maintenance, which usually targets specific volumes or uses interactive mode.

candidates.title: PowerShell Add-MpPreference Exclusion Paths And Disable Realtime Monitoring
candidates.rationale: The PowerShell command adding two specific exclusion paths (C:\PerfLogs and C:\ProgramData\AnyDesk) and disabling real-time monitoring in a single line is a deliberate defense evasion action. The Defender operational event (5007) captures this configuration change. The conjunction of Add-MpPreference -ExclusionPath (twice) and Set-MpPreference -DisableRealtimeMonitoring $true is highly distinctive.
candidates.false_positive_risks: Administrators may add exclusions, but adding two paths in one command and immediately disabling real-time monitoring is extremely rare. The specific paths C:\PerfLogs and C:\ProgramData\AnyDesk further reduce false positives.

candidates.title: Svchost Execution With Rclone Parameters Targeting Mega
candidates.rationale: The binary svchost.exe (renamed Rclone) executed from C:\PerfLogs with a command line containing rclone-specific flags ('copy', 'mega:', '--transfers', '--config', '--ignore-existing') is a durable exfiltration behaviour. The masquerading name, the path shared with other intrusion artefacts, and the unique flag combination make this a high-fidelity single-event detection.
candidates.false_positive_risks: Legitimate Rclone use exists, but the binary renamed to svchost.exe, running from C:\PerfLogs, and using a config file in the same directory with Mega remote syntax is not standard practice. System processes named svchost.exe do not exist.

candidates.title: Msiexec Silent Install Of AnyDesk MSI From Temp Directory
candidates.rationale: The silent installation of AnyDesk via msiexec.exe with /i pointing to an MSI in the user's Temp directory and /qn flag, followed by AnyDesk.exe --set-password, establishes an unauthorized persistent remote access channel. The msiexec.exe /i ... /qn pattern with an MSI in AppData\Local\Temp is highly specific to this intrusion's initial foothold.
candidates.false_positive_risks: Software deployment tools may use msiexec.exe /qn, but the source path C:\Users\svc_scanner\AppData\Local\Temp\AnyDesk.msi and the immediate follow-up AnyDesk.exe --set-password are not standard admin activity. The service account context (svc_scanner) further narrows scope.

skipped: B1: RDP password spraying - single-event rule on 4625/4624 would rely on volume or specific IP (IOC); better suited for analytic/threshold detection.
B4: Renamed Mimikatz mm.exe - binary name generic; path C:\PerfLogs overlaps with other rules but mm.exe alone lacks specificity without command-line arguments (none observed).
B5: Lateral movement via net use - net.exe is ubiquitous; the account adm-jpark is incident-specific, not a durable pattern.
B9: Stop services via net stop - less specific than B6's vssadmin/wbadmin/bcdedit; redundant inhibit-recovery coverage with lower fidelity.
plan.notes: Selected five rules spanning persistence, inhibit recovery, defense evasion (two), and exfiltration. All key on durable parent/child, command-line, or path constraints rather than indicators. Avoided multiple rules on same logsource with overlapping indicator sets; each candidate uses a distinct binary and command-line fingerprint.

rules.title: Remote Creation of WindowsUpdateHealth Task Pointing to Kestrel Encryptor
rules.sigma_yaml:
title: Remote Creation of WindowsUpdateHealth Task Pointing to Kestrel Encryptor
id: fb87a833-7e41-48bf-8bf9-c55205d6f920
status: experimental
description: 'Detects remote creation of a scheduled task named ''WindowsUpdateHealth'' via schtasks.exe that executes kstrl.exe
  from C:\PerfLogs as SYSTEM on start, indicative of Kestrel ransomware persistence.'
author: RuleSmith (Nemotron via Nebius Token Factory)
date: '2026-10-18'
tags:
- attack.persistence
- attack.t1053.005
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
  service: sysmon
detection:
  selection_image:
    'Image|endswith': '\schtasks.exe'
  selection_create:
    'CommandLine|contains|windash': /create
  selection_taskname:
    'CommandLine|contains': WindowsUpdateHealth
  selection_taskrun:
    'CommandLine|contains': 'C:\\PerfLogs\\kstrl.exe'
  condition: selection_image and selection_create and selection_taskname and selection_taskrun
falsepositives:
- Unknown
level: high

tests.label: positive
tests.description: Positive event: remote creation of WindowsUpdateHealth task executing kstrl.exe from PerfLogs as SYSTEM.

tests.label: positive
tests.description: Variant with different casing and parent process.

tests.label: negative

tests.label: positive
tests.description: Uses -create flag (windash), parameter reordering, extra whitespace, and PowerShell parent.

tests.label: positive
tests.description: All flags uppercase, tabs and extra spaces, SysWOW64 binary, WMI provider parent.

tests.label: positive
tests.description: Double extension on kstrl.exe (kstrl.exe.exe) preserves required substring, -create flag, cmd parent.

tests.label: positive
tests.description: Parameter reordering: /tn first, then /s, then /create; rundll32.exe parent (LOLBin).

tests.label: positive
tests.description: Excessive whitespace between all tokens, mshta.exe parent.

tests.label: negative
tests.description: Legitimate admin creates similarly named task 'WindowsUpdateHealthCheck' (different task name).

tests.label: negative

tests.label: negative

history.summary: 8 evasion variants -> positives 7/8, negatives blocked 6/6, benign hits 0/1200

history.change_summary: Fixed the task name detection to use simple substring match instead of quoted token to handle excessive whitespace in command line.

rules.author_notes: Rule focuses on the combination of remote task creation (/s), specific task name masquerading as Windows Update, unusual payload path (C:\PerfLogs\kstrl.exe), and SYSTEM privilege. Filters omitted as these traits together are highly suspicious; legitimate use rarely combines all four.
rules.redteam_analysis: Positive variants (P4-P8) demonstrate realistic operator evasions that preserve all four rule selections: they keep Image ending with \schtasks.exe, include a /create or -create flag (windash), contain the exact substring /tn "WindowsUpdateHealth" (case-insensitive match assumed per existing P2), and contain the exact substring "C:\PerfLogs\kstrl.exe" (with double quotes). Techniques used: flag spelling (-create), casing, whitespace, parameter reordering, double extension (kstrl.exe.exe still contains the target substring), alternate parent processes (PowerShell, WMI, rundll32, mshta), and SysWOW64 binary path. Negative variants (N1-N3) are benign look-alikes that differ in at least one selection: different task name, different target binary, or missing /create flag. Out-of-scope variants (O1-O6) represent evasions the current rule cannot catch because the logsource records literal strings that break one or more required substrings: renamed binary (no OriginalFileName), single quotes, 8.3 short names, UNC paths, environment variables, and different drive letters. A well-written rule would need additional fields (OriginalFileName, normalized path expansion) or broader path matching to cover O1, O3-O6; O2 would require accepting both quote styles. These are reported for analyst awareness.

redteam_out_of_scope.label: positive
redteam_out_of_scope.description: Renamed copy of schtasks.exe (evil.exe) - Image no longer ends with schtasks.exe, OriginalFileName not recorded by this logsource.

redteam_out_of_scope.label: positive
redteam_out_of_scope.description: Single quotes around task name and path - rule requires double quotes verbatim.

redteam_out_of_scope.label: positive

redteam_out_of_scope.label: positive
redteam_out_of_scope.description: UNC path to PerfLogs share - literal string differs from 'C:\PerfLogs\kstrl.exe'.

redteam_out_of_scope.label: positive
redteam_out_of_scope.description: Environment variable %SYSTEMDRIVE% - sensor records literal, not expanded.

redteam_out_of_scope.label: positive
redteam_out_of_scope.description: Different drive letter D: - rule keys on C:\PerfLogs\.

title: Vssadmin Delete Shadows All Quiet
id: e018c88d-dbef-4799-9d94-9f80603a0035
status: experimental
description: 'Detects vssadmin.exe execution with the exact arguments ''delete shadows /all /quiet'' which indicates ransomware

author: RuleSmith (Nemotron via Nebius Token Factory)

history.summary: 8 evasion variants -> positives 8/8, negatives blocked 6/6, benign hits 0/1200

rules.redteam_analysis: Positive variants P4-P8 demonstrate realistic operator evasions that a well-written rule should still catch: quoted full paths, 8.3 short names, environment-variable literals, SysWOW64 location, alternate parents (pwsh, wscript), and case/whitespace permutations. All preserve the four required CommandLine substrings and the OriginalFileName value, so the rule's 'contains|all' and equality checks succeed. Negative variants N1-N3 are benign administrative actions that differ in at least one required CommandLine token (/for=, list, resize) or ParentImage, proving specificity. Out-of-scope entries OOS1-OOS3 represent evasions the current rule cannot see because it keys on Image ending with \vssadmin.exe (renamed/relocated binary), or because the technique shifts to a different binary (wmic). These are reported for analyst awareness; extending coverage would require additional rules or broader Image logic.

redteam_out_of_scope.label: positive

rules.title: PowerShell Add-MpPreference Exclusion Paths And Disable Realtime Monitoring
rules.sigma_yaml:
title: PowerShell Add-MpPreference Exclusion Paths And Disable Realtime Monitoring
id: eaae235d-3605-48f6-9d1d-8dbd588de7c1
status: experimental
description: 'Detects PowerShell commands adding exclusion paths C:\\PerfLogs and C:\\ProgramData\\AnyDesk while disabling
  real-time monitoring via Set-MpPreference -DisableRealtimeMonitoring $true, captured as Windows Defender operational event
  ID 5007.'
author: RuleSmith (Nemotron via Nebius Token Factory)
date: '2026-10-18'
tags:
- attack.defense-evasion
- attack.t1562.001
logsource:
  category: file_event
  product: windows
  service: windefend
detection:
  selection_cmd:
    'CommandLine|contains|all':
    - Add-MpPreference

    - 'C:\\PerfLogs'

rules.author_notes: The rule targets the highly specific combination of adding two particular exclusion paths (C:\\PerfLogs and C:\\ProgramData\\AnyDesk) while disabling real-time monitoring in a single PowerShell command, as seen in Kestrel ransomware affiliate activity. This minimizes false positives by requiring all distinctive elements together. Test events include positives matching the observed command line variations and negatives representing legitimate administrative actions that lack either the specific paths or the concurrent real-time monitoring disablement.
rules.redteam_analysis: The five positive variants (P4-P8) preserve all seven required literal substrings in CommandLine while varying casing, whitespace, quoting style, binary location (pwsh.exe vs powershell.exe, System32 vs SysWOW64 vs custom path), parent process context, and adding benign prefix/suffix commands. A well-written rule using case-insensitive 'contains|all' on the CommandLine field will catch them. The three negative variants (N1-N3) represent legitimate administrative or installer activity: each misses at least one required substring (specific paths, the DisableRealtimeMonitoring flag, or the second exclusion path) and differs in CommandLine content, ensuring the rule stays specific. Four out-of-scope evasions (O1-O4) are realistic but fundamentally defeat the current rule's literal-string approach: environment variables and 8.3 short names change the recorded path string; splitting across multiple invocations prevents any single event from containing all substrings; -EncodedCommand obfuscates the entire payload. These require either path normalization, cross-event correlation, or command decoding — capabilities beyond the current rule's scope and logsource fields.

redteam_out_of_scope.label: positive
redteam_out_of_scope.description: Attacker uses environment variable %TEMP% expanded to C:\PerfLogs; sensor records literal %TEMP% so required substring C:\PerfLogs is absent.

event.Message: Windows Defender Antivirus configuration has been changed.

redteam_out_of_scope.label: positive
redteam_out_of_scope.description: Attacker uses 8.3 short name PERFLO~1 for C:\PerfLogs; sensor records the short name, required substring C:\PerfLogs not present.

event.Message: Windows Defender Antivirus configuration has been changed.

redteam_out_of_scope.label: positive
redteam_out_of_scope.description: Attacker splits into three separate PowerShell invocations; each event lacks the full set of required substrings, rule only sees per-event CommandLine.

event.Message: Windows Defender Antivirus configuration has been changed.

redteam_out_of_scope.label: positive
redteam_out_of_scope.description: Attacker uses -EncodedCommand with base64 payload; CommandLine shows encoded string, required plaintext substrings absent.

event.Message: Windows Defender Antivirus configuration has been changed.

rules.title: Rclone Disguised as Svchost Exfiltrating to Mega
rules.sigma_yaml:
title: Rclone Disguised as Svchost Exfiltrating to Mega
id: b4fc82f7-337f-4aa1-b4c8-c8516242f1e0
status: experimental
description: 'Detects svchost.exe (renamed Rclone) executing from C:\PerfLogs with rclone copy command targeting a Mega remote,
  indicative of data exfiltration.'
author: RuleSmith (Nemotron via Nebius Token Factory)
date: '2026-10-18'
tags:
- attack.exfiltration
- attack.t1048.003
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
  service: sysmon
detection:
  selection_img:
    'Image|endswith': '\svchost.exe'
  selection_dir:
    CurrentDirectory: 'C:\PerfLogs'
  selection_cli:
    'CommandLine|contains|all':
    - copy
    - 'mega:'
    - --transfers
    - --config
    - --ignore-existing
  condition: 'all of selection_*'
falsepositives:
- Legitimate use of svchost.exe for system services
- Authorized Rclone usage from non-standard locations
- Administrative scripts using svchost.exe naming for legitimate tasks
level: high

history.summary: 7 evasion variants -> positives 7/7, negatives blocked 6/6, benign hits 0/1200

rules.redteam_analysis: Positive variants P4-P7 demonstrate realistic operator evasions: flag casing changes (--CONFIG, --TRANSFERS), flag reordering, UNC source paths, quoted config paths, SysWOW64 binary location, PowerShell parent, and environment variables recorded literally (%USERPROFILE%). All preserve the five required command-line substrings and the exact CurrentDirectory value 'C:\PerfLogs', so a well-written rule on this logsource catches them. Negative variants N1-N3 are benign look-alikes: genuine svchost.exe from System32 with service flags, legitimate rclone from Program Files targeting OneDrive, and SCCM-cached rclone with different working directory; each differs in at least one rule field (Image path, CurrentDirectory, or command-line substrings). Out-of-scope variants OOS1-OOS4 represent evasions the current rule logic fundamentally cannot detect without loosening selections into noise: binary rename breaking the Image suffix, changed CurrentDirectory, different cloud remote (gdrive:), or dropping a required flag. These are recorded for the analyst to decide whether separate rules or enriched telemetry (e.g., OriginalFileName) are warranted.

redteam_out_of_scope.label: positive
redteam_out_of_scope.description: Binary renamed to svhost.exe (typo) so Image no longer ends with svchost.exe; rule keys on Image suffix

redteam_out_of_scope.label: positive
redteam_out_of_scope.description: Execution from C:\PerfLogs\Subdir so CurrentDirectory differs; sensor records exact directory

redteam_out_of_scope.label: positive

redteam_out_of_scope.label: positive

rules.title: Msiexec Silent Install of AnyDesk MSI from Temp Directory
rules.sigma_yaml:
title: Msiexec Silent Install of AnyDesk MSI from Temp Directory
id: 6df300ce-7e8e-4f9c-b86d-230982bf6955
status: experimental
description: Detects silent installation of AnyDesk via msiexec with /i and /qn flags from a user Temp directory, indicative
  of unauthorized remote access deployment.
author: RuleSmith (Nemotron via Nebius Token Factory)
date: '2026-10-18'
tags:
- attack.defense-evasion
- attack.t1218.011
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
  service: sysmon
detection:
  selection_msiexec:
    'Image|endswith': '\msiexec.exe'
  selection_cmd:
    'CommandLine|contains|all':
    - msiexec.exe
    - /i
    - /qn
  selection_path:
    'CommandLine|contains': '\AppData\Local\Temp\AnyDesk.msi'
  filter_normal:
    'ParentImage|contains|all':
    - '\Microsoft Configuration Manager\'
    - '\ccmsetup.exe'
  condition: selection_msiexec and selection_cmd and selection_path and not filter_normal
falsepositives:
- Legitimate software deployment via SCCM/Intune using msiexec /qn from internal distribution points.
level: medium

tests.description: Silent install of AnyDesk MSI from Temp directory via msiexec with /qn flag

tests.label: positive

tests.label: positive

tests.label: negative

validation.sql: SELECT * FROM logs WHERE Image LIKE '%\\msiexec.exe' ESCAPE '\' AND (CommandLine LIKE '%msiexec.exe%' ESCAPE '\' AND CommandLine LIKE '%/i%' ESCAPE '\' AND CommandLine LIKE '%/qn%' ESCAPE '\') AND CommandLine LIKE '%\\AppData\\Local\\Temp\\AnyDesk.msi%' ESCAPE '\' AND (NOT COALESCE((ParentImage LIKE '%\\Microsoft Configuration Manager\\%' ESCAPE '\' AND ParentImage LIKE '%\\ccmsetup.exe%' ESCAPE '\'), 0))

conversions.elasticsearch: Image:*\\msiexec.exe AND (CommandLine:*msiexec.exe* AND CommandLine:*\/i* AND CommandLine:*\/qn*) AND CommandLine:*\\AppData\\Local\\Temp\\AnyDesk.msi* AND (NOT (ParentImage:*\\Microsoft\ Configuration\ Manager\\* AND ParentImage:*\\ccmsetup.exe*))

| where FolderPath endswith "\\msiexec.exe" and (ProcessCommandLine contains "msiexec.exe" and ProcessCommandLine contains "/i" and ProcessCommandLine contains "/qn") and ProcessCommandLine contains "\\AppData\\Local\\Temp\\AnyDesk.msi" and (not((InitiatingProcessFolderPath contains "\\Microsoft Configuration Manager\\" and InitiatingProcessFolderPath contains "\\ccmsetup.exe")))
conversions.sqlite: SELECT * FROM logs WHERE Image LIKE '%\\msiexec.exe' ESCAPE '\' AND (CommandLine LIKE '%msiexec.exe%' ESCAPE '\' AND CommandLine LIKE '%/i%' ESCAPE '\' AND CommandLine LIKE '%/qn%' ESCAPE '\') AND CommandLine LIKE '%\\AppData\\Local\\Temp\\AnyDesk.msi%' ESCAPE '\' AND (NOT COALESCE((ParentImage LIKE '%\\Microsoft Configuration Manager\\%' ESCAPE '\' AND ParentImage LIKE '%\\ccmsetup.exe%' ESCAPE '\'), 0))

history.summary: 8 evasion variants -> positives 8/8, negatives blocked 6/6, benign hits 0/1200

rules.author_notes: Rule focuses on the combination of msiexec /i /qn with AnyDesk MSI in Temp directory to minimize false positives from legitimate deployments. ParentImage filter excludes common SCCM/Intune sources. The rule assumes Sysmon logs full command line including executable name.
rules.redteam_analysis: Positive variants (P4–P8) preserve the literal substrings the rule requires: Image ends with \msiexec.exe, CommandLine contains msiexec.exe, /i (or /I), /qn (or /QN), and the exact path fragment \AppData\Local\Temp\AnyDesk.msi. They vary casing, parameter order, whitespace, quoting, parent process, drive letter, and binary location (SysWOW64, copied binary retaining the msiexec.exe name) — all surface changes a well-written rule should normalize. Negative variants (N1–N3) are benign look-alikes that differ in at least one recorded field: N1 matches the SCCM filter (ParentImage contains both \Microsoft Configuration Manager\ and \ccmsetup.exe), N2 and N3 use different MSI filenames or paths so selection_path fails. Out-of-scope variants (OOS1–OOS4) represent realistic evasions the current rule cannot catch because the sensor records the literal string (%TEMP%, 8.3 short names, renamed binary without OriginalFileName, different MSI name) and the rule's selections demand the exact expanded path and binary name. A more robust rule would use OriginalFileName, path normalization, or a broader MSI-name pattern, but those changes belong to rule hardening, not to this test set.

redteam_out_of_scope.label: positive
redteam_out_of_scope.description: Environment variable %TEMP% expands to AppData\Local\Temp at runtime but sensor records literal %TEMP%; rule's selection_path requires literal \AppData\Local\Temp\AnyDesk.msi

redteam_out_of_scope.label: positive
redteam_out_of_scope.description: 8.3 short name APPDAT~1 for AppData; sensor records short name verbatim, rule needs \AppData\Local\

redteam_out_of_scope.label: positive
redteam_out_of_scope.description: Renamed/copied binary (evil.exe) — Image no longer ends with \msiexec.exe; OriginalFileName would reveal it but this logsource/rule does not use OriginalFileName

redteam_out_of_scope.label: positive
redteam_out_of_scope.description: Different MSI filename (AnyDesk_v2.msi) — attacker goal changes; rule keys on AnyDesk.msi specifically
